titleEn: The Song of the Cid — At Cardeña: Ximena's plea, and Castilians gather to follow the Cid (tiradas 15–17, lines 242–294)
part: Tiradas 15–17 · At Cardeña: Ximena's plea, and Castilians gather to follow the Cid (lines 242–294)

sentences.t:
Llamavan a la puerta, i sopieron el mandado;
Dios, qué alegre f[o] el abbat don Sancho!
sentences.l:
They-were-knocking at the gate, and they-learned the news;
God, how glad was the abbot don Sancho!
sentences.i: They knocked at the gate, and the news was known within: God, how glad the abbot don Sancho was!
sentences.n: Tirada 15 (assonance á-o) — the Çid is welcomed at San Pedro de Cardeña, entrusts his wife and daughters to the abbot with money for their keep, and Ximena kneels to him in tears. Every line-ending carries á-o (mandado, Sancho, salto, nasco … braços, amos, manos, nado, echado); nasco fits with its stressed a and final o, as in tirada 11. Llamavan, imperfect, then sopieron, preterite (of saber, 'came to know'): the subject shifts unannounced from the Çid's party knocking outside to the monks who hear who it is. mandado = 'message, news'. Dios, qué alegre … ! is the narrator's own exclamation, the minstrel breaking in; the same opening as the burghers' cry at v. 20, but there it was quoted speech. f[o] = fue, 3rd sg. preterite of ser, with its o restored by Pidal. el abbat don Sancho is the abbot met at matins in v. 237.

sentences.t:
Con lu[m]bres e con candelas al corral dieron salto,
con tan grant gozo reçiben al que en buen ora nasco.
sentences.l:
With lights and with candles to-the courtyard they-gave leap,
with so great joy they-receive the-one who in good hour was-born.
sentences.i: With torches and candles they rushed out into the courtyard; with such great joy they receive him who was born in a good hour.
sentences.n: lu[m]bres are lights, torches or lamps, the m restored by Pidal; the night office is just over and it is not yet day. corral = the walled courtyard of the monastery, not a farmyard. dieron salto, 'gave a leap', i.e. sprang out, rushed out. dieron (preterite) then reçiben (present): epic tense-mixing, the present pulling the welcome into the listener's view. al que en buen ora nasco: the birth-form of the formula, 'him who was born in a good hour'; nasco, strong preterite of nasçer (= nació).

sentences.t:
“Gradéscolo a Dios, mio Çid”, dixo el abbat don Sancho;
“pues que aquí vos veo, prendet de mí ospedado.”
sentences.l:
“I-thank-it to God, my Çid”, said the abbot don Sancho;
“since here you I-see, take from me lodging.”
sentences.i: “I thank God for it, my Çid,” said the abbot don Sancho; “since I see you here, take lodging from me.”
sentences.n: Gradéscolo = lo agradezco, 1st sg. present with lo glued on: the enclitic squeeze, 'I thank (God) for it'. The abbot too says mio Çid, as Ximena did at v. 241. pues que = 'since'. prendet is the 2nd pl. imperative of prender 'to take' (modern prended, tomad), the final -d spelt -t as often in the manuscript; vos is the polite plural to one man. ospedado = hospedaje, 'lodging, hospitality', spelt without h.

sentences.i: The Çid said, he who was born in a good hour: “Thanks, lord abbot, and I am well content with you. I shall make ready provisions for myself and for my vassals;
sentences.n: The whole second half of v. 248, [el que en buen ora nasco], is Pidal's restoration, and the next line, which he counts as 248b, keeps the traditional numbering undisturbed. so vuestro pagado = 'I am pleased with you, content with you': so = soy, vuestro 'your' has the force 'with you', and pagado, past participle of pagar in its old sense 'to satisfy, please' (pagarse de, 'to be pleased with'), not 'paid'. don abbat: don is the title of respect, 'lord abbot'. adobaré is the simple future of adobar 'to make ready, prepare'; conducho = 'provisions, food for the journey'. pora = para. mi[o]s, with the o restored by Pidal, is the full masculine plural possessive mios, as in mios enemigos at v. 9. The Çid declines to live on the house: he will feed his own men.

sentences.t:
mas por que me vo de tierra, dovos çinquaenta marcos,
si yo algún día visquier[o], se[e]rvos han doblados.
sentences.l:
but because myself I-go from land, I-give-you fifty marks,
if I some day should-live, to-be-to-you they-will doubled.
sentences.i: But since I am going out of the land, I give you fifty marks; if I live to see the day, they shall be doubled to you.
sentences.n: por que = 'because'; me vo = me voy, 1st sg. present of ir with the reflexive, 'I go away'. de tierra, 'out of the land', the stock phrase for exile, without the article. dovos = os doy, 1st sg. present of dar with vos glued on. visquier[o] is the future subjunctive of vivir on its strong stem visc- (the preterite visque), with its final o restored by Pidal: si yo algún día visquiero, 'if I live (on) some day', i.e. if I come through. se[e]rvos han doblados is a split future: the infinitive seer (= ser, its second e restored by Pidal), then vos, then han, = os serán doblados, 'they will be doubled to you'. The same construction as mereçer no' lo hedes at v. 197, here with ser.

sentences.t: Non quiero far en el monesterio un dinero de daño;
sentences.l: Not I-want to-do in the monastery one penny of damage;
sentences.i: I will not do the monastery one penny's worth of harm;
sentences.n: far is the short form of fazer, as at v. 229. un dinero, 'one penny': the dinero (Latin denarius) was the smallest silver coin, so a dinero de daño is 'a pennyworth of loss'. The Çid will not let his household be a charge on the monks.

sentences.t:
evades aquí pora doña Ximena dovos çient marcos;
a ella e a sus fijas e a sus dueñas sirvádeslas est año.
sentences.l:
see-here here for doña Ximena I-give-you hundred marks;
to her and to her daughters and to her ladies serve-them this year.
sentences.i: see, here for doña Ximena I give you a hundred marks; serve her and her daughters and her ladies this year.
sentences.n: evades is a presentative, 'look, here you have', akin to afevos at v. 262 (afé + vos); with aquí it points to the money being handed over, and the line then says it again in plain terms, dovos çient marcos. The exact make-up of the form is not certain. çient = cien, ciento cut short before its noun. a ella e a sus fijas e a sus dueñas … sirvádeslas: the object is named three times with a and then taken up again by las glued to the verb, a doubling the poem uses freely (Dámosvos … a vos, v. 196). sirvádeslas = que las sirváis, present subjunctive used as a polite command. est año = este año, the -e lost before the vowel. The Çid expects his exile to last at least a year.

sentences.i: I leave two daughters, little girls: take them in your arms. Here I commend them to you, abbot don Sancho; take every care of them and of my wife.
sentences.n: Dues = dos, the old feminine form of 'two', agreeing with fijas. niñas stands as a predicate, 'I leave them (as) little girls', young children. prendetlas = prendedlas, imperative + las, as prendet at v. 247: 'take them in your arms', i.e. into your keeping. [las] is Pidal's restoration; acomiendo = encomiendo, 'I entrust'. vos … a vos marks the person twice, as Dámosvos … a vos at v. 196. fagades is the present subjunctive of fazer used as a command, 'may you take, do take'; todo recabdo, 'every care' (cf. con grand recabdo, v. 24). mugier = mujer, 'wife'. The daughters will be named later in the poem; here they have no names.

sentences.i: If that provision runs short for you, or you lack anything, keep them well supplied — I charge you so; for every mark you spend, I will give the monastery four.”
sentences.n: essa despenssa is the hundred marks just given, the money for their keep (despensa = 'spending, provision'). falleçiere, menguare are future subjunctives of falleçer 'to fail, run out' and menguar 'to be lacking', the normal mood of an open condition (as fiziéredes, f[o]re at v. 223). bien las abastad: abastad is the 2nd pl. imperative of abastar 'to supply, keep provided'; the pronoun las comes before the imperative because bien stands in front of it, an order modern Spanish does not allow. yo assí vos lo mando, 'I so command you' — mandar here 'to order', not 'to promise' as at vv. 180, 224. despendades = gastéis, present subjunctive of despender 'to spend'. al monesterio belongs with daré: 'I will give the monastery four'. The Çid, who has just borrowed six hundred marks on chests of sand, promises fourfold repayment with a lord's ease.

sentences.t: Otorgado gelo avie el abbat de grado.
sentences.l: Granted it-to-him had the abbot willingly.
sentences.i: The abbot had granted it to him willingly.
sentences.n: Otorgado gelo avie: aver in the imperfect (avie, as at v. 22) + past participle, a pluperfect, 'had granted', with the participle fronted for weight. gelo = ge lo, 'it to him', as gelos at v. 186. de grado = 'gladly, willingly'.

sentences.t:
Afevos doña Ximena con sus fijas do va ilegando;
señas dueñas las traen e adúzenlas [en los braços].
sentences.l:
Behold-you doña Ximena with her daughters where she-goes arriving;
each-a lady them carry and bring-them [in the arms].
sentences.i: And here is doña Ximena coming up with her daughters; a lady apiece carries them, bringing them along in their arms.
sentences.n: Afevos = 'behold, here you have', the presentative afé with vos, the minstrel pointing his listeners to the scene. do = donde. va ilegando: ir + gerund, 'she is coming up, drawing near'. The word is read as llegando ('arriving'); Pidal's print has ilegando, with a plain dotted i for the first letter, most likely a misprint (cf. llegó, v. 236; llególas, v. 276), and the text here follows the print. señas = 'one each' (Latin singulas), a distributive: each little girl is carried by a lady of her own. traen, adúzenlas: traer and aduzir (= aducir) 'to bring' set side by side, the second with las glued on. The second half of v. 263, [en los braços], is Pidal's restoration, echoing prendetlas en los braços at v. 255. The ladies are the five dueñas de pro of v. 239.

sentences.t:
Ant el Campeador doña Ximena fincó los inojos amos.
Llorava de los ojos, quísol besar las manos:
sentences.l:
Before the Campeador doña Ximena planted the knees both.
She-was-weeping from the eyes, she-wanted-to-him to-kiss the hands:
sentences.i: Before the Campeador doña Ximena went down on both her knees. She wept, and sought to kiss his hands:
sentences.n: Ant = ante, 'before'. fincó los inojos = she knelt: fincar = hincar 'to drive in, plant', with initial f- for modern h-, and inojos = hinojos 'knees' (Latin genuculum). amos = ambos, 'both'. Llorava de los ojos, 'wept from the eyes', is the poem's weeping formula, the words that open its first surviving line (De los sos ojos … llorando). quísol = quísole, 'she wanted to (kiss) him the hands': the le is the person whose hands they are, glued to the verb with its e lost. Kissing the lord's hands is the gesture of one asking a boon, as Raquel's at v. 179.

sentences.t:
“Merçed, Canpeador, en ora buena f[o]stes nado!
Por malos mestureros de tierra sodes echado.
sentences.l:
“Mercy, Campeador, in hour good you-were born!
By wicked slanderers from land you-are cast-out.
sentences.i: “Mercy, Campeador, you who were born in a good hour! It is wicked talebearers that have had you cast out of the land.
sentences.n: Ximena's speech opens here and runs on across the tirada break to v. 273: the change of assonance falls in the middle of her words. Merçed, 'mercy, grace', is the word of a petitioner, a plea rather than thanks. Canpeador is spelt with n, as at v. 175. en ora buena f[o]stes nado is the birth-form of the formula with its words turned about: f[o]stes = fuistes, 2nd pl. preterite of ser with its o restored by Pidal, and nado = nacido, the old past participle of nasçer. mestureros = 'talebearers, slanderers' (mestura, 'denunciation'): the enemigos malos of v. 9, who accused the Çid before the king. sodes = sois; sodes echado is the passive, 'you are cast out', echado singular, agreeing with the one man addressed by the polite plural.

sentences.t:
Merçed, ya Çid, barba tan complida!
Fem ante vos yo e vuestras ffijas,
iffantes son e de días chicas,
con aquestas mis dueñas de quien so yo servida.
sentences.l:
Mercy, O Çid, beard so full!
Behold-me before you I and your daughters,
children they-are and of days small,
with these my ladies of whom am I served.
sentences.i: Mercy, O Çid, beard so full! Here I am before you, I and your daughters — they are children, and young in days — with these my ladies by whom I am served.
sentences.n: Tirada 16 (assonance í-a) — Ximena asks the Çid for counsel; he takes his daughters in his arms and prays to live to marry them. The new assonance comes in the middle of her speech, which began at v. 266; every ending carries í-a (complida, ffijas, chicas, servida … remanida, María, vida, servida). ya is the vocative 'O' (cf. Ya Campeador, v. 41). barba tan complida, 'beard so full': the full beard is the mark of the Çid's manhood and honour, and the poem names him by it; complida = cumplida, 'perfect, complete'. Fem = heme, 'behold me, here I am': the presentative fe (as in afé) with me glued on. ffijas and iffantes are spelt with a doubled ff, kept as printed. iffantes = 'children' (the word also names young men of noble birth, as it will later in the poem); de días chicas, 'small of days', young. Pidal numbers the third line 269b. aquestas = estas. de quien so yo servida, 'by whom I am served': quien refers to the plural dueñas, since it had no plural form; so = soy.

sentences.t:
Yo lo veo que estades vos en ida
e nos de vos partir nos hemos en vida.
Dadnos consejo por amor de santa María!”
sentences.l:
I it see that are you on departure
and we from you to-part ourselves we-will in life.
Give-us counsel for love of holy Mary!”
sentences.i: I see that you are on the point of going, and we must be parted from you while we live. Give us counsel, for the love of holy Mary!”
sentences.n: Yo lo veo que …: lo anticipates the que-clause, 'I see it, that …'. estades = estáis; en ida, 'on the way out, departing'. nos … partir nos hemos is a split future (= nos partiremos): the first nos is the subject 'we' (= nosotros), the second the reflexive, set between the infinitive and hemos, the present of aver. en vida, 'in life', i.e. while both live — a parting like death. consejo is 'counsel' but also 'help, provision, a way through', what a lord owes those in his keeping. The speech that opened at v. 266 ends here.

sentences.t:
Enclinó las manos la barba vellida,
a las su[e]s fijas en braço' las prendía,
llególas al coraçón, ca mucho las quería.
sentences.l:
Lowered the hands the beard handsome,
to the his daughters in arm(s) them he-was-taking,
he-drew-them to-the heart, for much them he-loved.
sentences.i: He of the handsome beard reached down his hands; he took his daughters in his arms and drew them to his heart, for he loved them dearly.
sentences.n: la barba vellida, 'the handsome beard', stands for the Çid himself, the subject of Enclinó; vellida = bellida, 'fair, handsome'. Enclinó las manos is uncertain: most likely he stretches his hands down to the kneeling Ximena and the children (to raise her, or to take the girls); a gesture of bowing is not ruled out, but the next line favours reaching down for the daughters. a las su[e]s fijas: article + possessive, with sues the old feminine plural of 'his' and its e restored by Pidal; the a marks the persons, then las takes them up again. braço' = braços, the s lost before las (the apostrophe marks the dropped letter, as no' at v. 192). prendía, imperfect, between the preterites enclinó and llególas: tense-mixing. llególas = las llegó, 'drew them close' (llegar transitive, 'to bring near'). ca = 'for'; quería, 'loved'.

sentences.t:
Llora de los ojos, tan fuerte mientre sospira:
“Ya doña Ximena, la mi mugier tan complida,
commo a la mi[e] alma yo tanto vos quería.
sentences.l:
He-weeps from the eyes, so strong-ly he-sighs:
“O doña Ximena, the my wife so perfect,
as to the my soul I so-much you loved.
sentences.i: He weeps, and sighs so deeply: “Ah, doña Ximena, my wife so perfect, I have loved you as dearly as my own soul.
sentences.n: Llora de los ojos, the weeping formula, now in the present (Ximena's at v. 265 was imperfect). tan fuerte mientre = tan fuertemente: -mientre is the old form of the adverb ending -mente, here printed apart from its adjective (cf. fuertemientre, v. 1). sospira = suspira. Ya doña Ximena, vocative 'O'. la mi mugier, article + possessive; complida, 'perfect', the word Ximena used of his beard at v. 268, now given back to her. commo a la mi[e] alma: mie is the feminine of mio, its e restored by Pidal, 'as my own soul'. quería, the imperfect, 'I have loved you, I have always loved you': a love of long standing, not a past one.

sentences.t:
Ya lo ve[e]des que partir nos emos en vida,
yo iré y vos fincaredes remanida.
sentences.l:
Now it you-see that to-part ourselves we-will in life,
I shall-go and you will-stay left-behind.
sentences.i: Now you see that we must part while we live: I shall go, and you will remain behind.
sentences.n: Ya here is 'now', not the vocative. ve[e]des = veis, the second e restored by Pidal. partir nos emos is the same split future as Ximena's at v. 272, his answer taking up her words; emos is hemos without the h. fincaredes = quedaréis, the future of fincar 'to remain' (f- for modern h-, as fincó at v. 264); remanida, past participle of remaner 'to stay behind', agreeing with Ximena. y is here taken as 'and' (as at v. 13); it can also mean 'there' (as at v. 239), so 'I shall go, and there you will remain' is not ruled out.

sentences.t:
Plega a Dios e a santa María,
que aun con mis manos case estas mis fijas,
e quede ventura y algunos días vida,
e vos, mugier ondrada, de mí seades servida!”
sentences.l:
May-it-please to God and to holy Mary,
that yet with my hands I-may-marry these my daughters,
and may-remain fortune and some days life,
and you, wife honoured, by me may-you-be served!”
sentences.i: May it please God and holy Mary that I may yet with my own hands give these my daughters in marriage, and that fortune and some days of life be left me; and that you, my honoured wife, be served by me!”
sentences.n: Plega is the present subjunctive of plazer, 'may it please'. case is the present subjunctive of casar, transitive 'to give in marriage': a father married his daughters 'with his own hands' when he himself made the match and gave them away, and the wish looks forward to the business of the poem's later cantares. Pidal numbers the line 282b. estas mis fijas, demonstrative + possessive together, as aquestas mis dueñas at v. 270. quede, present subjunctive of quedar, 'may remain (for me)'; ventura y algunos días vida, 'fortune and some days of life' — y again as 'and', and vida without de after algunos días. ondrada = honrada. seades, present subjunctive of seer (= seáis); de mí seades servida, 'may you be served by me', returning Ximena's own words at v. 270, de quien so yo servida: he hopes to come back and maintain her as a lord should.

sentences.t:
Grand yantar le fazen al buen Canpeador.
Tañen las campanas en San Pero a clamor.
sentences.l:
Great meal to-him they-make for-the good Campeador.
They-ring the bells in San Pero at full-peal.
sentences.i: They make a great feast for the good Campeador. The bells of San Pedro ring out in full peal.
sentences.n: Tirada 17 (assonance ó) — the news of the exile spreads through Castile, and a hundred and fifteen knights gather at the Arlanzón bridge and ride to join the Çid at San Pedro. The tirada rhymes on stressed ó (Canpeador, clamor, Arlançón, son, cojó, naçió), and twice on ó-e (pregones, onores), which counts as the same assonance, as in tirada 14. yantar, the infinitive used as a noun, is 'a meal', properly the midday dinner. le fazen, with the dative le taken up by al buen Canpeador. Tañen las campanas … a clamor: a clamor is a loud, full peal; whether they ring in his honour or as a summons the line does not say. San Pero = San Pedro de Cardeña.

sentences.i: Throughout Castile the cries are heard going round, that my Çid the Campeador is leaving the land; some leave their houses, and others their honours.
sentences.n: o[d]iendo = oyendo, gerund of oír, its d restored by Pidal. The construction of van … o[d]iendo los pregones is not certain: either the people of Castile 'go hearing the proclamations' (an unnamed subject, with los pregones as object), or the proclamations themselves 'go about being heard'. pregones are public cries, announcements made aloud in town and village; what is cried is the news in the next line, commo se va de tierra mio Çid — commo = 'how, that'; se va, 'he is going away'. onores, 'honours', are lands and revenues held as a fief, a tenure from the king; to leave them to follow an exile is to forfeit them, as Martín Antolínez knew his goods were forfeit (v. 230). unos … otros, 'some … others'.

sentences.i: On that day, at the bridge over the Arlanzón, a hundred and fifteen knights are gathered all together; all are asking for my Çid the Campeador.
sentences.n: aqués = aquese, 'that'. la puent is feminine, as puente often was in Old Spanish; Arla[n]çón is the river of Burgos (vv. 55, 201), its n restored by Pidal. çiento quinze = ciento quince. juntados son, 'are gathered', ser + participle, with the verb last for the assonance. demandan por, 'they ask after, seek'. Campeador here with m, Canpeador at v. 288 with n: both spellings stand as printed.

sentences.t:
Martín Antolínez con ellos' cojó.
Vansse pora San Pero do está el que en buen[a] naçió.
sentences.l:
Martín Antolínez with them joined-himself.
They-go-off toward San Pero where is the-one who in a-good (hour) was-born.
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez joined them. They set off for San Pedro, where he is who was born in a good hour.
sentences.n: con ellos' cojó = con ellos se cogió, 'joined himself to them': the apostrophe marks the se, swallowed after the s of ellos (as no' at v. 192 and braço' at v. 275 mark a lost s). cojó, preterite of coger, in the sense 'to join, fall in with', spelt with j. Martín Antolínez, back from Burgos as he promised at v. 231, comes with the new men. Vansse = vanse, 'they go off', the s doubled. do = donde. el que en buen[a] naçió: the birth-form of the formula with ora left unsaid, 'in a good (hour)', buen[a] with its a restored by Pidal (as in en buen[a] çinxiestes espada); naçió is the regular preterite, beside the strong nasco of vv. 245, 248.
